fact_en: The rough texture of abaca fibers increases friction! This makes them perfect for tying heavy loads securely.
fact_bis: Ang garbong nga texture sa abaca fibers mopataas sa friction! Mao nga maayo kini gamiton sa pag-ukit sa bug-at nga karga nga lig-on.

findings.note: Two substitutions gut the card. (1) "Ang GARBONG nga texture sa abaca fibers mopataas sa friction" — garbo = pride/elegance, not rough; the correct word magaspang is used in ffct-28006's own title for the identical "rough surface increases friction" fact, so the causal reason (roughness) is simply absent here and the title ("Friction sa Abaka") restores nothing. (2) "maayo kini gamiton sa PAG-UKIT sa bug-at nga karga" — ukit = to carve/engrave; EN is "tying heavy loads" (paghigot/pagbugkos), so the application fact is replaced by a different thing. A child reads that abaca's elegant texture is good for carving heavy loads.

fact_en:
How does a simple circuit light a bulb?

When you close the switch, electrical energy flows through the wire to light the bulb!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagpailaw sa bombilya sa yano nga circuit?

Kung isira nimo ang switch, moagi ang electrical energy sa wire aron mapalong ang bombilya!

findings.note: Outcome reversed: "Kung isira nimo ang switch, moagi ang electrical energy sa wire aron MAPALONG ang bombilya" = closing the switch makes the bulb GO OUT. EN is "to light the bulb". Palong = extinguish — confirmed inside this same batch, where ffct-27935 uses "mapalong ang tanang suga" for "all the lights go out". The answer sentence teaches the opposite of the circuit fact; the question header ("pagpailaw") only makes it contradictory, not recoverable.

fact_en: Kids playing on a wooden seesaw at Rizal Park in Manila use a first-class lever to easily lift each other up and down!
fact_bis: Ang mga bata nga nagdula sa kahoy nga seesaw sa Rizal Park sa Manila naggamit ug first-class lever aron sayon ra nila buhaton ang usag usa!

findings.note: title_bis "Sip-sip nga Lever" for "Seesaw Lever": sip-sip in Cebuano means to SUCK/sip, it is not a seesaw. Strongest evidence the title is the outlier: this card's own body keeps the English word ("kahoy nga seesaw sa Rizal Park") and the sibling card ffct-28120 also keeps "seesaw". The title names a different object; the body is fine.

fact_en: A strong neodymium magnet easily attracts iron nails, but it completely ignores aluminum soda cans and pure copper wires!
fact_bis: Ang kusog nga neodymium magnet dali ra makadani sa mga pako nga puthaw, pero dili makaapekto sa aluminum nga lata ug copper nga mga kable!

findings.note: Third instance of the same swap: "makadani sa mga pako nga puthaw" for "attracts iron nails". Cebuano pako = wing/fern, not lansang (nail). The contrast with aluminum and copper survives, but the object the magnet picks up is named as an iron wing and is never corrected in the card.

fact_en: Pop a copper nail and a zinc nail into a squeezed calamansi—and boom! You just made a tiny electrical current!
fact_bis: Isuksok ang copper nga pako ug zinc nga pako sa gipiga nga calamansi—ug wow! Nakahimo ka og gamay nga electrical current!

findings.note: Same false friend, and here it breaks a hands-on instruction: "Isuksok ang copper nga pako ug zinc nga pako sa gipiga nga calamansi" for "pop a copper nail and a zinc nail into a squeezed calamansi". Cebuano pako = wing/fern (nail = lansang). The card never names the object any other way, so a child cannot carry out or picture the calamansi-battery demo.

fact_en: In the water cycle, gravity is the pulling force that makes precipitation fall from clouds back to Earth's surface!
fact_bis: Sa water cycle, ang gravity mao ang puwersa nga nagahuyop nga maoy hinungdan nga ang precipitation mohulog gikan sa panganod paingon sa yuta!

findings.note: EN: "gravity is the PULLING force that makes precipitation fall". BIS: "ang gravity mao ang puwersa nga NAGAHUYOP" — huyop = to BLOW (with breath/air). The card's science point is that gravity pulls; the Cebuano states the opposite kind of force (blowing/pushing air) and never says bira/dani anywhere, unlike the neighbouring gravity cards (ffct-28107 "i-pull", ffct-28110 "gipull", ffct-28159 "nagbira"). Lower confidence than the flags above because the clause "precipitation mohulog gikan sa panganod paingon sa yuta" still keeps the downward direction.

fact_en: The Pacific electric ray in Philippine coral reefs generates sudden electrical currents to stun small fish before eating them!
fact_bis: Ang Pacific electric ray sa mga coral reef sa Pilipinas nagpagawas og kalit nga electrical currents aron patindog ang gagmay nga isda una kaunon!

findings.note: EN: the electric ray "generates sudden electrical currents to STUN small fish before eating them". BIS: "nagpagawas og kalit nga electrical currents aron PATINDOG ang gagmay nga isda una kaunon" — patindog = to make (something) STAND UP / erect. The effect of the shock is the whole point of the card, and the Cebuano states a different effect that nothing else in the card corrects (stun = palipong / paralisahon).

fact_en: Liquid water can actually boil at room temperature if you lower the surrounding air pressure enough using a simple vacuum pump!
fact_bis: Ang likidong tubig pwede mokulo sa room temperature kung ibanan nimo ang pressure sa hangin gamit ang yano nga vacuum pump!

findings.note: title_bis "Kulob Room Temp" for "Boiling at Room Temp": Cebuano kulob = lying FACE-DOWN / overturned; to boil is kulo. The card's own body has the correct verb ("pwede MOKULO sa room temperature"), which is exactly the pattern of a title outlier — the title heading the boiling-at-room-temperature fact says something about being upside-down instead.

fact_en: The Philippine gumamela (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) has bright red petals! These petals reflect red light wavelengths to beautifully attract pollinating butterflies.
fact_bis: Ang Philippine gumamela (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) adunay hayag nga pula nga mga talong! Nag-reflect kini sa red light wavelengths aron makadani sa mga pollinating butterflies.

findings.note: EN: gumamela "has bright red petals". BIS: "adunay hayag nga pula nga mga talong" — talong is an EGGPLANT, not a petal (Cebuano petal = petalo / mga dahon sa bulak). The card then says "Nag-reflect KINI sa red light wavelengths", so the red eggplants are also the thing that reflects red light and attracts butterflies. Nothing in the card (title is only "Pula Gumamela") restores "petal", so a child reading only the Cebuano learns that a hibiscus grows red eggplants.

fact_en:
How do you make a temporary magnet out of an iron nail?

During magnetization, you stroke the nail with a permanent magnet! This aligns its internal magnetic domains in the same direction.
fact_bis:
Unsaon paghimo og temporary magnet gikan sa pako nga puthaw?

Sa proseso sa magnetization, ihaplas kini gamit ang permanent magnet! Mag-align kini sa internal magnetic domains sa parehas nga direksyon.

findings.note: Tagalog false friend, and it is in the TITLE as well as the body: title_bis "Pagmamagnet sa Pako" and body "temporary magnet gikan sa pako nga puthaw". In Cebuano pako = WING (pakô) / edible FERN (pakû); a nail is lansang. The whole card is an instruction about an iron nail, and the word is never corrected anywhere in the card — the child is told to stroke an iron wing with a magnet.

fact_en: Gravity pulls mature Philippine coconuts downward from tall palm trees! They need a strong, hard shell to protect the seed during the fall.
fact_bis: Ang gravity nagbira sa mga hamtong nga Philippine coconuts paingon sa ilawom gikan sa taas nga kahoy! Kinahanglan ug lig-on nga shell aron maprotektahan ang liso samtang nagahulog.

findings.note: title_bis "Lubog Niyog Shell" for "Coconut Fall Shells": lubog in Cebuano means MURKY/turbid (Tagalog: submerged/sunken) — it does not mean falling. The body has the correct word ("samtang NAGAHULOG", "nagbira ... paingon sa ilawom"), and the rest of this batch uses lubi for coconut (ffct-28106, ffct-28148, ffct-28217) while only this title uses the Tagalog niyog — both signs the title is the outlier.

fact_en:
What is fluid friction or drag?

It occurs when objects move through liquids like water or gases like air, slowing them down!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang fluid friction o drag?

Mahitabo kini kung ang mga butang molihok sa likido sama sa tubig o gas sama sa hangin!

findings.note: The card asks "Unsa ang fluid friction o drag?" and the EN answer is "It occurs when objects move through liquids like water or gases like air, SLOWING THEM DOWN!" The Cebuano stops at "kung ang mga butang molihok sa likido sama sa tubig o gas sama sa hangin!" and drops the slowing-down effect entirely — the defining property the card exists to teach. A child reading only the Cebuano cannot answer what drag actually does.
